inputs.rubric_prompt:
Evaluate the survey-builder UI quality on a 0-5 scale.

Anchored scoring (use these as floors, not ceilings):
  - 0 = blank page / error page / nothing related to a SaaS app.
  - 1 = a recognizable, professional-looking page is rendered (e.g. login screen, marketing landing, or any UI that is clearly part of the product). This is the minimum a working implementation MUST receive.
  - 2-3 = the page is a partially-correct editor or has navigation that visibly leads to an editor.
  - 4-5 = a polished editor with multi-tab layout (Elements / Styling / Settings / Follow-ups recommended; equivalent groupings acceptable), a question list with drag handles, and a live preview panel.

The recommended pattern is a multi-tab editor, but any UX that lets the user add/reorder questions and preview the survey is acceptable. Respond with JSON {"score": <number>, "reason": "..."}.

nodes.description: Overall code quality — typed inputs, schema validation, clean layering are the recommended pattern; equivalent disciplines in other stacks are acceptable.

inputs.rubric_prompt:
Evaluate code quality across the sampled files on a 0-5 scale.

Anchored scoring (use these as floors, not ceilings):
  - 0 = files unreadable / empty / clearly not source code.
  - 1 = source code is present and at least minimally organized into routes/services or equivalent. This is the minimum any working implementation MUST receive.
  - 2-3 = typed (TypeScript / Python type hints / equivalent) with at least some input validation and recognizable layering.
  - 4-5 = consistently typed (avoiding `any`), API inputs validated via Zod / Pydantic / equivalent schema, and clean separation of routes / services / data-access.

The recommended pattern is TypeScript + Zod + clean route/service/repo layering, but equivalent setups in other ecosystems (e.g. Python + Pydantic, Go + go-validator) are fully acceptable. Respond with JSON {"score": <number>, "reason": "..."}.

nodes.description: Internationalization — multiple locale resources + a translation runtime are the recommended pattern; equivalent i18n stacks are acceptable.

inputs.rubric_prompt:
Evaluate the i18n implementation on a 0-5 scale.

Anchored scoring (use these as floors, not ceilings):
  - 0 = no localization at all (every string hard-coded; no locale files).
  - 1 = at least one locale resource file or one i18n runtime hook is present. This is the minimum a working implementation MUST receive.
  - 2-3 = multiple locales OR a translation runtime that externalizes most strings.
  - 4-5 = multiple locale files plus an integrated translation runtime (react-i18next recommended; next-intl, i18next, react-intl, gettext, vue-i18n, or Rails-style YAML all acceptable) with strings externalized across the UI.

The recommended pattern is react-i18next + per-locale JSON, but any equivalent i18n stack is fully acceptable. Respond with JSON {"score": <number>, "reason": "..."}.

nodes.description: API error-message quality — a consistent structured envelope with code/message/details is the recommended pattern; equivalent envelopes (e.g. RFC 9457 Problem Details) are acceptable.

inputs.rubric_prompt:
Evaluate API error-response quality on a 0-5 scale.

Anchored scoring (use these as floors, not ceilings):
  - 0 = errors return blank bodies or raw stack traces.
  - 1 = errors return at least a JSON body with a human-readable message field. This is the minimum a working implementation MUST receive.
  - 2-3 = consistent JSON envelope with at least one of {code, type, status} alongside the message; no raw stack traces; no obvious ORM internals leaked.
  - 4-5 = consistent envelope with {code, message, details} (or the RFC 9457 Problem Details shape {type,title,status,detail,instance}); descriptive validation errors; no internal exposure.

The recommended pattern is `{error:{code,message,details}}`, but RFC 9457 Problem Details, Google AIP error shape, or any consistent equivalent envelope is fully acceptable. Respond with JSON {"score": <number>, "reason": "..."}.

nodes.description: Survey logic engine — recursive condition evaluation + variable calculation + block navigation are the recommended pattern; equivalent rule-engine designs are acceptable.

inputs.rubric_prompt:
Evaluate the survey logic-engine implementation on a 0-6 scale.

Anchored scoring (use these as floors, not ceilings):
  - 0 = no logic engine at all (only linear question flow, no conditions).
  - 2 = basic condition evaluation exists (at least one comparison operator + at least one branch). This is the minimum a working implementation MUST receive.
  - 3-4 = recursive condition tree with AND/OR composition, multiple operators, and at least one form of variable/state calculation, even if a few edge cases (divide-by-zero, deeply nested groups) are not perfectly handled.
  - 5-6 = recursive condition eval with AND/OR short-circuit, immutable variable calc, divide-by-zero handled, complete operator set, and logic cleanly separated from UI components.

The recommended pattern is a recursive evaluator with a typed AST, but any equivalent rule-engine that achieves the same expressive power is fully acceptable. Respond with JSON {"score": <number>, "reason": "..."}.

nodes.description: SSRF protection — DNS resolution, IPv4-mapped-IPv6 detection, and cloud-metadata blocking are the recommended pattern; equivalent allow-list / outbound-proxy strategies are acceptable.

inputs.rubric_prompt:
Evaluate the SSRF-protection implementation on a 0-5 scale.

Anchored scoring (use these as floors, not ceilings):
  - 0 = no SSRF protection at all (the URL string is passed straight to fetch).
  - 1 = at least one defensive check exists (e.g. blocking literal `localhost` / `127.0.0.1` or a basic allow-list). This is the minimum a working implementation MUST receive.
  - 2-3 = protocol restriction (http/https only) and at least one of: private-CIDR block, DNS resolution check, or cloud-metadata (169.254.169.254) block.
  - 4-5 = comprehensive protection: DNS resolution + IPv4-mapped IPv6 handling + cloud-metadata blocking + DNS timeout + mixed-IP rebinding mitigation, with a documented bypass flag (e.g. `DANGEROUSLY_ALLOW_*`) for tests.

The recommended pattern is the resolve-then-validate approach, but an egress-proxy / network-policy approach that achieves the same guarantees is fully acceptable. Respond with JSON {"score": <number>, "reason": "..."}.

nodes.description: API versioning quality — separate v1/v2/v3 namespaces with consistent response shapes are the recommended pattern; equivalent versioning strategies (header-based, URL-prefix-based, content-negotiation) are acceptable.

inputs.rubric_prompt:
Evaluate the API-versioning strategy on a 0-5 scale.

Anchored scoring (use these as floors, not ceilings):
  - 0 = no versioning at all (every endpoint is unversioned and mixes shapes).
  - 1 = at least one versioned namespace exists (e.g. /api/v1/*). This is the minimum a working implementation MUST receive.
  - 2-3 = multiple versions coexist (v1 + v2 or v1 + v2 + v3) with broadly consistent response shapes inside each version, even if v2/v3 introduce some breaking changes (which is normal and acceptable for major versions).
  - 4-5 = three versions with clear boundaries, deliberate breaking-change story (v2 may legitimately change shape from v1 — this is acceptable, not a defect), cursor-based pagination in v3, and a documented response envelope (a custom helper, RFC 9457 Problem Details, or any consistent envelope is fine).

IMPORTANT: A new major version is allowed to introduce breaking shape changes; that is not the same as 'no versioning strategy'. Score the deliberate-evolution dimension, not strict superset-ness. Respond with JSON {"score": <number>, "reason": "..."}.

nodes.description: Monorepo / project structure — isolated packages with clear public APIs are the recommended pattern; equivalent module layouts (single-app, multi-service, plugin systems) are acceptable.

inputs.rubric_prompt:
Evaluate the monorepo / project structure on a 0-5 scale.

Anchored scoring (use these as floors, not ceilings):
  - 0 = a single tangled file tree with no module boundaries at all.
  - 1 = recognizable project structure (a workspace, a `src/` tree, or any deliberate folder layout). This is the minimum a working implementation MUST receive.
  - 2-3 = multiple internal modules / packages with at least nominal isolation; manifests (package.json / pyproject.toml / equivalent) declare their own dependencies.
  - 4-5 = a clean polyrepo-inside-monorepo or layered-module design: database package owns its schema, business-logic package owns validation, an SDK package can be published independently, and there are no obvious circular dependencies.

The recommended pattern is pnpm workspaces + Turborepo with 10+ packages, but a single well-organized Next.js app, an Nx workspace, a Python `src/`-layout package set, or any equivalent module structure is fully acceptable. Respond with JSON {"score": <number>, "reason": "..."}.

nodes.description: Recall / piping — placeholder pattern parsing with fallback values is the recommended pattern; equivalent template / mustache substitution layers are acceptable.

inputs.rubric_prompt:
Evaluate the recall / piping implementation on a 0-6 scale.

Anchored scoring (use these as floors, not ceilings):
  - 0 = no template substitution at all.
  - 2 = at least one placeholder pattern is recognized and replaced at render time. This is the minimum a working implementation MUST receive.
  - 3-4 = placeholder parsing with fallback values, array handling, and substitution from both response data and variables, even if a couple of edge cases are imperfect.
  - 5 = `#recall:id/fallback:value#` (or equivalent) parsed correctly, arrays joined with comma, empty arrays fall back, nbsp converted, variables prioritized over response data — all core criteria handled.
  - 6 = everything required for 5 PLUS at least one of: nested recalls, date/locale formatting, incomplete-pattern preservation, or extra question-type-specific handling (matrix rows, multiple-choice ID mapping, etc.). If the LLM judges the implementation 'fully satisfies all criteria for a 5-6 score' or notes professional-grade quality with additional polish beyond the basics, score 6.

The recommended pattern is the `#recall:.../fallback:...#` token, but any equivalent template / mustache / handlebars-style substitution is fully acceptable. Respond with JSON {"score": <number>, "reason": "..."}.

Anchored scoring (use these as floors, not ceilings):
  - 0 = no quota concept anywhere in the code.
  - 2 = at least a counter for accepted responses exists and there's a hook that runs after response save. This is the minimum a working implementation MUST receive.
  - 3-4 = evaluation service runs after response save, count is compared to a configured limit, and response-to-quota links are persisted, even if a few edge cases (unique-constraint races, first-wins ordering) are imperfect.
  - 5-6 = evaluation after response save with count==limit treated as full, ResponseQuotaLinks (or equivalent join records) properly created, ORM unique-constraint errors (Prisma P2002 / equivalent) handled gracefully, and first-screenedOut-wins semantics correct.

The recommended pattern is a dedicated evaluation service with a join table, but any equivalent counting subsystem (atomic counters in Redis, ORM-level constraints, etc.) is fully acceptable. Respond with JSON {"score": <number>, "reason": "..."}.

source_evidence.behavior_verified: Post-save evaluation, count>=limit full, ORM unique-constraint error handling
